title: Watch Water Resistance Ratings Explained: 3 ATM to 20 ATM
meta_description: What 3 ATM, 5 ATM, 10 ATM and 20 ATM watch ratings really mean, why 30 m is not a diving depth, and how to keep gaskets sealed over time.
intro: The water resistance figure printed on a watch dial or case back is one of the most misread specifications in accessories. A watch marked 30 meters is not designed to be taken 30 meters underwater, and a rating that was accurate on the day of purchase can quietly stop being true a few years later. Knowing how these ratings are tested, what each tier is realistically suited for, and which habits break a seal helps you choose the right watch and avoid a fogged or flooded movement.

sections.heading: How Water Resistance Ratings Are Measured
sections.body:
Water resistance is expressed in three interchangeable ways: meters, bar, or ATM (atmospheres). One bar or one ATM corresponds to roughly 10 meters of static water pressure, so 5 ATM, 5 bar, 50 m and WR50 all describe the same rating. The key word is static. The figure describes the pressure a stationary watch withstood in a test, not the depth a person can safely take it while moving.

The main reference for everyday watches is ISO 22810, which sets out testing for watches sold as water resistant, including immersion, condensation and pressure checks. Dive watches are covered by a separate and stricter standard, ISO 6425, which requires at least 100 meters plus extra requirements such as a timing bezel, legibility in darkness, and resistance to shock and magnetism. A watch marked 200 m without dive-specific features meets a pressure figure, but it is not automatically a certified diver.

Real-world use adds dynamic pressure. Swinging an arm through water, diving into a pool, or being hit by a wave briefly raises the load on the seals. That gap between test conditions and real life is why manufacturers recommend activities far shallower than the number on the dial.

sections.heading: What Each Rating Is Realistically Suited For
sections.body:
Manufacturers publish their own guidance, and the owner's manual should always take priority, but the common tiers line up fairly consistently across the industry.

A 3 ATM or 30 m rating covers everyday splashes: rain, washing hands and accidental spills. It is not intended for swimming or showering. Many dress watches and minimalist designs fall into this category.

A 5 ATM or 50 m rating handles brief immersion and, in many manufacturers' guidance, light surface swimming, though some still advise against swimming at this level. Many smartwatches carry this rating.

A 10 ATM or 100 m rating is generally considered the practical minimum for regular swimming, snorkeling and surface water sports. Most sports and field watches aim for this level.

A 20 ATM or 200 m rating suits high-speed water sports, surfing and skin diving, and is common on rugged digital and sport models. For scuba diving, the safer choice is a watch explicitly certified to ISO 6425 and labeled as a diver's watch.

A watch with no water resistance marking at all should be kept away from water entirely.

sections.heading: Why Water Resistance Fades Over Time
sections.body:
Water resistance depends on rubber or synthetic gaskets compressed around the case back, crystal, crown and pushers. These seals are consumable parts. Over time they dry out, flatten and lose elasticity, especially when exposed to heat, sunscreen, perfume, chlorine and salt. A watch rated 100 m when new may resist far less pressure after several years without service.

Mechanical events also compromise seals. Opening the case to replace a battery can disturb or pinch the case-back gasket, which is why reputable repairers reseal and often pressure-test the watch afterward. A hard knock can shift the crystal slightly, and a crown left pulled out, or a screw-down crown left unscrewed, gives moisture a direct path inside.

Heat is a specific threat. Hot showers, saunas and hot tubs make metal and gaskets expand at different rates, and steam penetrates small gaps more easily than liquid water. Moving a warm watch into cold water can also create condensation inside the case. Many service centers suggest a pressure test about once a year for watches worn in water regularly, and always after the case has been opened.

sections.heading: Habits That Keep a Watch Sealed
sections.body:
A few simple rules prevent most water damage. Never pull out the crown or press chronograph pushers underwater unless the manual explicitly allows it, since operating them opens a path through the seal. If the watch has a screw-down crown, confirm it is screwed fully in before every swim.

After swimming in the sea or a chlorinated pool, rinse the watch under cool fresh water and dry it with a soft cloth. Salt crystals and chlorine residue accelerate gasket wear and can corrode bracelets and pins. Leather straps should be kept dry altogether, because water and sweat stiffen and crack leather regardless of the case rating.

Avoid wearing a non-diver watch in hot tubs and saunas, and let a warm watch cool to room temperature before plunging it into cold water. If fog appears under the crystal, moisture is already inside; take the watch to a repairer promptly rather than waiting for it to clear, because trapped humidity corrodes movements and dials. Finally, ask for a pressure test whenever the battery is changed, which is the most practical moment to replace aging gaskets.

faq.q: Can I shower with a 5 ATM watch?
faq.a: Some manufacturers permit it, but hot water, steam and soap are hard on gaskets, and pressing buttons under the spray adds risk. If the manual is silent or advises against it, removing the watch before showering is the safest habit, especially on older watches whose seals have not been serviced recently.

faq.q: Is a water resistant watch the same as waterproof?
faq.a: No. Watch standards avoid the word waterproof because no watch stays sealed indefinitely; gaskets age and can be disturbed by impacts or battery changes. Water resistant means the watch passed pressure testing at a specified level when made. Its real protection depends on its condition, service history and how it is used.

faq.q: What rating do I need for swimming laps?
faq.a: For regular swimming, 10 ATM (100 m) is the widely recommended practical minimum, because arm strokes and pool push-offs create dynamic pressure beyond the static test level. A 20 ATM rating adds margin for diving into pools, surfing and snorkeling. Check that any screw-down crown is fully closed before getting in.

faq.q: How often should water resistance be tested?
faq.a: For watches worn in water regularly, many service centers suggest a pressure test about once a year. Any watch should also be tested after the case back is opened, such as for a battery change, and after a hard impact. The test is quick and many repairers can do it with dry air pressure equipment.

title: How to Wash Linen Without Shrinking or Damaging It
meta_description: Why linen shrinks and wrinkles, the right water temperature, how to dry and iron it, and how to care for linen-cotton and linen-viscose blends.
intro: Linen shorts, pants and summer dresses are prized for being cool and breathable in hot weather, but linen also has a reputation for shrinking in the first wash and creasing the moment it is worn. Both behaviors come directly from the structure of the flax fiber. Once you understand why linen reacts to heat, agitation and folding the way it does, washing it becomes straightforward, and well-cared-for linen tends to get softer and more comfortable with every wash.

sections.heading: Why Linen Shrinks and Wrinkles
sections.body:
Linen is woven from flax, a plant fiber made mostly of cellulose, the same basic material as cotton. Flax fibers are long, stiff and highly crystalline, which gives linen its strength, crisp feel and good moisture wicking. The same structure means the fiber has very little elasticity. When linen is bent or compressed, hydrogen bonds between cellulose chains reform in the new shape, and with little natural spring back, a crease stays put.

Shrinkage is mostly relaxation shrinkage. During spinning and weaving, yarns are held under tension. The first time the fabric is soaked, especially in hot water with vigorous agitation, those yarns relax and draw closer together, so the garment gets shorter and narrower. Heat from a tumble dryer compounds the effect. Most of this shrinkage happens in the first one or two washes.

This is why fabric labeled pre-washed, pre-shrunk, garment-washed or stonewashed usually behaves more predictably: the relaxation was triggered during manufacturing. Crisp unwashed linen and loosely woven linen are the most likely to change size, so treat a new piece conservatively until it has been washed once.

sections.heading: Washing Linen: Temperature, Cycle and Detergent
sections.body:
Start with the care label. In the United States, most apparel must carry one under the FTC Care Labeling Rule, and it reflects what the whole garment, including linings and trims, is expected to tolerate. Where the label allows machine washing, a few settings make a large difference.

Use cool to lukewarm water, roughly 30 to 40 degrees Celsius, rather than hot. Choose a gentle or delicate cycle with a reduced spin speed, since aggressive tumbling drives shrinkage and abrades the fiber along seams and folds. Leave plenty of space in the drum; linen absorbs a lot of water and becomes heavy, and an overloaded machine creases it deeply.

A mild liquid detergent rinses out more completely than powder in cool water. Avoid chlorine bleach, which weakens cellulose fibers and can cause yellowing; for white linen, an oxygen-based bleach used as directed is gentler. Fabric softener is unnecessary, because linen softens naturally with washing, and softener residue can reduce its absorbency.

Turn dark or brightly dyed linen inside out and wash it with similar colors, since linen tends to lose dye along creases where the fibers flex most.

sections.heading: Drying and Ironing Linen the Right Way
sections.body:
Drying is where much linen shrinkage and stiffness happens. Air drying is the safest option: shake the garment out firmly as soon as the cycle ends, smooth the seams and hems with your hands, and hang it on a padded hanger or lay it flat. Dry dark linen out of direct sun to limit fading. Line-dried linen can feel stiff at first, but it softens quickly once worn.

If a dryer is used, choose low heat and remove the item while it is still slightly damp. Over-drying makes linen feel brittle and sets wrinkles that are much harder to remove.

Linen tolerates more heat than most fabrics and corresponds to the highest setting on most irons, but it irons best while damp. Press a slightly damp garment, or use steam or a spray bottle, working on the reverse side of dark fabrics to avoid shine. For a softer, relaxed look, many people skip ironing and hang linen in a steamy bathroom or use a handheld steamer. Some wrinkling is a natural characteristic of the fabric, not a sign of poor quality.

sections.heading: Caring for Linen Blends and Storing Linen
sections.body:
Many linen shorts and pants are blends, most commonly linen with cotton, viscose (rayon) or a small percentage of elastane. A blend should be washed according to its most delicate fiber. Linen-cotton blends behave much like pure linen but wrinkle a little less. Viscose is noticeably weaker when wet and prone to shrinking, so linen-viscose garments benefit from cold water, a gentle cycle or hand washing, and drying flat. Elastane, which adds stretch to waistbands and fitted styles, is damaged by high heat, so avoid hot washes, hot dryers and very hot irons on those pieces.

Storage matters because of the fiber's stiffness. Flax fibers can weaken where the same sharp fold is pressed repeatedly over long periods, so hanging or rolling linen, and varying fold lines, helps prevent wear along creases. Store linen clean and fully dry, since body oils and moisture left in the fabric encourage yellowing and mildew. A breathable cotton garment bag is better than sealed plastic for long-term storage, and starch should be washed out before seasonal storage because it can attract insects.

faq.q: Can I make linen shrink on purpose if it is too big?
faq.a: A warm wash followed by a dryer cycle on medium heat will often tighten linen that has not been pre-washed, but the result is uneven and hard to control, and it can stiffen the fabric. Pre-shrunk linen changes little. For a meaningful size change, tailoring is far more predictable than heat.

faq.q: Can linen be washed in a machine?
faq.a: Most linen garments can be machine washed if the care label allows it. Use cool to lukewarm water, a gentle cycle with a low spin, a mild detergent and a loosely filled drum. Structured items such as lined linen blazers, or blends with viscose, may still require dry cleaning or hand washing.

faq.q: Why does my linen feel stiff after air drying?
faq.a: As linen dries without movement, its cellulose fibers set in place, which gives a crisp, slightly stiff feel. It softens within minutes of wear, or you can tumble it briefly on a cool or air-only setting when nearly dry. The fabric generally becomes softer over time with repeated washing.

faq.q: Is it normal for linen to wrinkle so easily?
faq.a: Yes. Flax fiber has very little elastic recovery, so it holds folds and creases. Linen-cotton blends and fabrics with a small amount of elastane wrinkle somewhat less. Many people accept the relaxed texture as part of linen's character, and steaming smooths it quickly when a crisper look is wanted.

title: Why Sterling Silver Tarnishes and How to Clean It Safely
meta_description: What 925 sterling silver really is, why it turns yellow or black, safe cleaning methods for each level of tarnish, and storage habits that slow it.
intro: Sterling silver earrings, rings and bracelets are popular because they offer the look of a precious metal at an accessible price, yet many owners are surprised when a bright piece turns yellow, gray or black in a drawer. Tarnish is not a sign that the silver is fake or poor quality; it is a normal chemical reaction on the surface of the metal. Understanding what causes it makes it easy to choose the gentlest cleaning method for each piece and to store jewelry so tarnish forms more slowly.

sections.heading: What Sterling Silver Actually Is
sections.body:
Pure silver, often called fine silver, is too soft for most jewelry, so it is alloyed with other metals for strength. Sterling silver is an alloy of 92.5 percent silver, with copper typically making up most of the remaining 7.5 percent. That is why sterling pieces are stamped 925, .925, Sterling or Ster. In the United States, the FTC Guides for the Jewelry, Precious Metals, and Pewter Industries state that an item should be described as sterling silver only if it contains at least 925 parts per thousand of pure silver.

It helps to distinguish sterling from look-alike terms. Silver-plated means a thin layer of silver over a base metal, and the plating can wear through with polishing. Silver-tone or silver-colored describe appearance only and indicate no silver content. Some sterling jewelry is also plated with rhodium, a hard, bright platinum-group metal that resists tarnish; these pieces look very white and stay bright longer, but the plating can wear thin with time.

Knowing which of these you own matters, because cleaning methods suited to solid sterling can strip plating or damage decorative finishes.

sections.heading: The Chemistry of Tarnish
sections.body:
Tarnish forms mainly when silver reacts with sulfur compounds in the air, such as hydrogen sulfide, producing a thin film of silver sulfide. At first the film appears as a faint yellow or golden tint; as it thickens it turns brown, then gray and eventually black. The copper in sterling can also oxidize and add to the discoloration. Because tarnish is a surface layer, it can be removed without harming the underlying metal if the right method is used.

Several everyday conditions speed the reaction. Humidity is a major accelerator, which is why jewelry kept in a bathroom tarnishes quickly. Common sulfur sources include rubber bands, latex, wool, felt, some paper and cardboard, and foods such as eggs and onions. Perspiration, lotions, perfumes and hair products leave residues that react with the metal, and chlorinated pool or hot tub water can discolor and corrode silver alloys.

Pieces worn frequently often tarnish less than pieces left in a box. Gentle friction against skin and clothing removes the earliest film before it builds up, as long as the jewelry is wiped clean after contact with sweat or cosmetics.

sections.heading: Cleaning Methods From Gentlest to Strongest
sections.body:
Always start with the mildest method that works. For light tarnish and everyday grime, wash the piece in warm water with a few drops of mild dish soap, use a very soft brush for crevices, rinse well and dry completely with a lint-free cloth.

For moderate yellowing or gray patches, a dedicated silver polishing cloth is the next step. These cloths contain a mild polishing compound; rub with straight, gentle strokes rather than circles, and move to a clean area of the cloth as it darkens.

For heavy tarnish on solid sterling without stones, the aluminum foil method converts silver sulfide back into silver through an electrochemical reaction rather than scraping metal away. Line a heat-safe bowl with aluminum foil, add baking soda and hot water, and submerge the jewelry so it touches the foil. After a few minutes, rinse and dry the piece thoroughly.

Commercial dip cleaners act quickly by dissolving tarnish chemically, but repeated use can leave the surface dull, so rinse thoroughly and use them sparingly. Avoid toothpaste and gritty scrubs, which are abrasive and leave fine scratches on polished silver.

sections.heading: Pieces That Need Special Care, and Storage That Prevents Tarnish
sections.body:
Some jewelry should not go into a chemical dip or foil bath. Oxidized sterling, where recesses have been deliberately darkened to highlight a design, will lose that contrast. Pearls, opals, turquoise, coral and other porous or soft gemstones can be damaged by chemicals and hot water, and stones set with adhesive may loosen. Rhodium-plated and silver-plated items are best cleaned only with soap, water and a soft cloth to avoid wearing through the plating. For antique or valuable pieces, a professional jeweler is the safest option.

Prevention is easier than removal. Store each piece separately in a small airtight zip bag or a lined box to limit air exposure and prevent scratches from harder jewelry. Anti-tarnish strips or cloths absorb sulfur compounds, and a small silica gel packet helps control humidity. Keep silver out of bathrooms and away from rubber bands and wool.

As a daily habit, put silver jewelry on after applying lotion, perfume and hairspray, remove it before swimming, cleaning with household chemicals or heavy exercise, and wipe each piece with a soft cloth before putting it away.

faq.q: Does tarnish mean my sterling silver is fake?
faq.a: No. Genuine sterling silver tarnishes because of its silver and copper content, so tarnish is consistent with real sterling. Items that never tarnish may be rhodium-plated sterling, stainless steel or another alloy. Look for a 925 or Sterling stamp, and remember that silver-tone describes color only, not silver content.

faq.q: Why does sterling silver sometimes turn my skin green or black?
faq.a: Dark marks usually come from tarnish rubbing off onto skin, often encouraged by sweat, humidity or cosmetics. Green marks typically come from the copper in the alloy reacting with moisture and acids on the skin. Both are generally harmless and wash off, and keeping the jewelry clean and dry reduces the effect.

faq.q: Is the aluminum foil and baking soda method safe?
faq.a: For solid sterling without stones or decorative oxidation, it is considered one of the gentlest ways to remove heavy tarnish, because it converts silver sulfide back to silver instead of abrading metal. Avoid it for plated pieces, pearls, porous gemstones, glued settings and intentionally darkened designs, and rinse and dry thoroughly afterward.

faq.q: Can I wear sterling silver in the shower or pool?
faq.a: Occasional contact with plain water will not ruin sterling, but frequent showering speeds tarnish through soap residue and humidity. Chlorinated pools and hot tubs are harsher and can discolor or corrode the alloy. Removing silver jewelry before swimming and bathing, then storing it dry, keeps it bright much longer.

title: How to Make Swimsuits Last: Chlorine, Sun and Care Tips
meta_description: Why chlorine, sunscreen and heat wear out swimsuit elastane, which fabrics resist pool chemicals, and the rinse and drying routine that helps suits last.
intro: Swimsuits, swim trunks and board shorts often look worn out long before they tear: the fabric bags at the seat, colors fade, the elastic goes slack, or a once-opaque suit turns slightly see-through. These problems rarely come from age alone. They are caused by specific, predictable stressors, mainly pool chlorine, ultraviolet light, sunscreen and heat. Understanding how swim fabrics are built and what breaks them down helps you choose the right suit for how you swim and keep it in good shape for more seasons.

sections.heading: What Swimwear Fabric Is Made Of
sections.body:
Most fitted swimsuits are knitted from nylon (polyamide) or polyester blended with elastane, also called spandex. Nylon is soft, smooth and stretchy, which is why it dominates fashion swimwear. Polyester feels slightly firmer but holds color well and is more resistant to chlorine and sunlight. Elastane provides stretch and recovery, letting a suit hug the body and spring back after it is pulled on; fitted suits commonly contain a substantial share of it, often somewhere around 15 to 20 percent.

Elastane is also the weakest link. It is a segmented polyurethane fiber, and chlorine, heat, oils and UV light all attack its structure. As the elastane degrades, the fabric loses recovery, which shows up as sagging, rippling and a loose fit, and the knit can thin until it becomes less opaque.

Loose swim trunks and quick-dry board shorts are usually woven polyester or nylon with little or no elastane, which is why they tend to survive pool and sun exposure better than fitted suits, although their colors and water-repellent finishes still fade with heavy use.

sections.heading: How Chlorine, Sun and Sunscreen Break Swimwear Down
sections.body:
Chlorine in pools is a strong oxidizer, which is exactly why it is used to sanitize water. The same oxidizing action breaks down elastane and fades many dyes. Damage accumulates every time a suit is worn and then left to dry with pool water still in the fibers, so a suit used for regular laps in a chlorinated pool can wear out far sooner than one worn occasionally at the beach. Hot tubs are harsher still, combining high temperatures with concentrated sanitizers.

Ultraviolet light causes photodegradation, fading dyes and weakening both elastane and nylon over time. Bright colors and suits left drying in direct sun are most affected.

Sunscreens, tanning oils and some insect repellents can leave yellow or orange stains on light fabrics, and oils can soften and degrade elastane. Some sunscreen ingredients can also react with minerals in water to create stubborn discoloration, so rinsing quickly matters.

Friction completes the picture. Sitting on rough pool edges, concrete or wooden decks causes pilling and snags, especially on the seat of a suit, and these abraded areas are where thinning appears first.

sections.heading: Choosing Swimwear for How You Swim
sections.body:
The best fabric depends on where and how often you swim. For occasional beach and vacation use, nylon-elastane suits offer comfort and a wide range of styles, and with good care they can last several seasons.

For frequent pool swimming, look for suits described as chlorine resistant. These are usually made of 100 percent polyester, polyester with PBT (polybutylene terephthalate, a polyester with some natural stretch), or blends using elastane engineered for higher chlorine resistance. They feel firmer and stretch less, but they hold their shape and color much longer in treated water. A stated fiber composition is more informative than a vague label, so check the content tag.

For sun protection, rash guards and swim shirts may carry a UPF rating, which measures how much ultraviolet radiation the fabric blocks. Standards such as AS/NZS 4399 classify UPF 50 and above as excellent protection, meaning the fabric lets through about one fiftieth or less of UV radiation. Fabric density and color affect protection, and stretched or worn fabric generally offers less, so a snug but not overstretched fit preserves both comfort and coverage.

sections.heading: A Care Routine That Extends Swimsuit Life
sections.body:
The single most effective habit is rinsing a suit in cool, clean water as soon as possible after swimming, ideally before it dries. This flushes out chlorine, salt, sand and sunscreen before they keep acting on the fibers.

Wash swimwear by hand in cool water with a small amount of mild detergent, or use a gentle machine cycle inside a mesh laundry bag if the care label permits. Avoid hot water, bleach and fabric softener, which all degrade elastane. Do not wring or twist the suit; instead, roll it in a towel and press to remove excess water.

Dry swimwear flat or over a rack in the shade, never in a clothes dryer and never on a hot radiator. Heat is one of the fastest ways to destroy elastane.

Rotating between two or more suits gives each one time to dry completely and the fibers time to recover between wears, which is commonly recommended for regular swimmers. Sit on a towel rather than directly on rough surfaces, let sunscreen absorb before dressing, and store clean, dry suits flat and away from sunlight.

faq.q: Why is my swimsuit becoming see-through?
faq.a: Thinning usually means the elastane and base fibers have been degraded by chlorine, heat or UV, and the knit has stretched and lost density. Areas under friction, such as the seat, are affected first. Once fabric has thinned this way it cannot be restored, so replacing the suit is the practical option.

For people who swim in chlorinated pools several times a week, they usually are. Polyester and PBT fabrics hold their shape and color far longer than standard nylon-elastane in treated water. They feel firmer and less stretchy, so for occasional beach wear a conventional suit is often more comfortable.

faq.q: Can I put a swimsuit in the washing machine?
faq.a: Some care labels allow a gentle, cool machine cycle, ideally with the suit inside a mesh laundry bag. Hand washing in cool water with mild detergent is gentler and is often recommended for padded or embellished suits. Always skip the dryer, because heat breaks down elastane quickly.

faq.q: How do I remove sunscreen stains from swimwear?
faq.a: Treat stains early. Rinse with cool water, then gently work a small amount of mild liquid detergent or dish soap into the mark and let it sit briefly before rinsing again. Avoid chlorine bleach, which damages elastane. Older yellow stains may be permanent, especially on white or pale fabrics.
